name: geis

attributes.attribute: king of Tara bound by sacred geasa
forbidden to eat the flesh of birds because his mother was enchanted into bird form
forbidden to ride around Tara with his right shoulder to the sea or to be away more than eight nights
pledged never to refuse a woman's advances
imposed geasa, often as surrogates of the goddess of Sovereignty
held to control the fertility of the land
pledged to avoid taboo places, people, and foods, with their strength tied to performance

sources: Dillon, Myles. There Was a King in Ireland: Five Tales from Oral Tradition. Texas Folklore Society. Austin: University of Texas Press, 1971, 21.
Joyce, Patrick Weston. Ancient Celtic Romances. London: Parkgate Books, 1997, 433–434.
Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: A geis is an Irish ritual vow, also written geas, geiss, or ges. Its plural is geasa or gessa. Kings and heroes made these magical pledges in ancient Irish literature. Druids or women imposed the geasa, never the men themselves. Some geasa had a clear reason. King Conaire of Tara could not eat the flesh of birds because his mother had been enchanted into bird form. Other geasa seemed trivial. Conaire also vowed not to ride around Tara with his right shoulder to the sea. He could not be away from Tara for more than eight nights. The hero Diarmait pledged never to refuse a woman's advances. Breaking a geis brought serious results, even death. The fertility of the land depended on the king's righteousness. A king who broke his geasa, like Conaire, left his land sterile. The performance of geasa bound the strength and even the life of heroes. These vows wound through many ancient Celtic legends.

okr.objective: Explain the Irish ritual vow of the geis and its force on kings and heroes.
